title: Limits on Punishment, a Brother's Duty, and Honest Weights
summary: Moses limits flogging to forty lashes, forbids muzzling an ox as it threshes, and sets out the duty of a brother-in-law to marry his brother's childless widow, with a public shaming ceremony for the man who refuses. He punishes a shameful act in a fight, requires honest weights and measures, and commands Israel to remember Amalek's attack on the weary stragglers in the wilderness.
story: This is the last chapter of the detailed laws in Deuteronomy's central code; chapter 26 closes the code with two ceremonies and a covenant declaration. The laws here continue the concerns of the previous chapters: the dignity of the guilty, the livelihood of the worker (even an animal), the survival of a family name, and honesty in trade. The chapter ends by looking back to one of the first battles after the exodus, Amalek's attack in Exodus 17, and forward to Israel's rest in the land. Several of these laws echo through the rest of the Bible: the brother-in-law duty shapes the stories of Tamar and of Ruth, and the ox law is quoted twice by Paul.
historical:
The Amalekites were a nomadic people of the southern desert regions, the Negev and Sinai. According to Exodus 17:8-16, they attacked Israel at Rephidim soon after the exodus, and Deuteronomy adds the detail that they struck the weary stragglers at the rear. They reappear as raiders in the time of the judges (Judges 6:3), and Saul's failure to carry out God's judgment on them and their king Agag cost him his kingdom (1 Samuel 15). The book of Esther calls its villain Haman an Agagite (Esther 3:1), and many interpreters, Jewish and Christian, have read that as a deliberate link to Amalek's king.

The practice of a brother marrying his dead brother's widow is called levirate marriage, from the Latin levir, brother-in-law. Similar customs are known from other ancient Near Eastern texts, including Hittite and Middle Assyrian laws. The earliest biblical example is the story of Judah's son Onan, who refused to give his brother Er an heir through Tamar (Genesis 38). The book of Ruth shows a related custom involving a more distant relative and the removal of a sandal (Ruth 4).
cultural:
In Israel, a man's name and his family's claim to its land passed through sons. A man who died childless was in danger of having his name blotted out and his land absorbed into another family, and his widow was left without support. The brother-in-law duty solved both problems: the first son of the new marriage would carry the dead brother's name and inherit his share. A brother who refused was, in effect, taking his brother's inheritance for himself. The ceremony at the gate shamed him publicly. The sandal was associated with the right to walk on and claim land, so removing it symbolized giving up that claim, and spitting in his face was a sign of contempt before the whole town.

Weights in the ancient world were stones carried in a bag, and measures were containers such as the ephah, used for grain. A merchant with a heavy stone for buying and a light one for selling could cheat every customer. The prophets repeatedly condemned this fraud (Amos 8:5; Micah 6:11). Oxen threshing grain walked in circles over the harvest on a threshing floor, and a muzzle kept them from eating as they worked.
literary: The chapter gathers unrelated laws, but they share a concern for fairness and dignity: the guilty man is not to be degraded, the ox is not to be denied food, the dead brother is not to lose his name, the customer is not to be cheated. The brother-in-law law includes spoken words at the gate, a small courtroom drama with speeches by the widow, the reluctant brother, and the widow again, ending with the nickname given to his family. The chapter closes with a command framed by remembering and blotting out, and the final words of verse 19 are a sharp imperative in Hebrew, two words long, which makes the forgetting itself the danger.

outline.t: Do not muzzle the threshing ox
A shameful act in a fight

doctrines.note: Justice in Israel has limits: even the guilty man is still your brother and must not be degraded. The law extends care to the working animal and demands honesty in the smallest transactions of trade.
The brother-in-law duty shows the family as a network of obligation. Protecting the dead man's name and the widow's future is a family responsibility, and refusing it is a public shame.
Amalek is judged for attacking the weak and weary, with no fear of God. God's judgment falls especially on those who prey on the vulnerable, and Israel is not to forget it.

words.note: Yabam, brother-in-law, and its related verb in verse 5, to perform the duty of a brother-in-law. The words are technical terms for levirate marriage. They describe not a romance but a duty undertaken for a dead brother's sake.

Na'al, sandal. The sandal carried legal meaning in Israel, connected with walking on land and claiming it. Removing it at the gate was a public renunciation, and the same gesture seals the land transaction between Boaz and the nearer relative in Ruth 4:7-8.

Even, stone, used here for a weight. Ancient weights were shaped stones, and verse 13 speaks literally of a stone and a stone, one large and one small. Proverbs 11:1 says a false balance is an abomination to the LORD, echoing the verdict of verse 16.

Amalek, the name of a people descended, according to Genesis 36:12, from Esau's grandson. In the Bible Amalek becomes a symbol of the enemy who attacks God's people at their weakest, and the command to remember what Amalek did is one of the few commands in the law to remember an enemy.

christ: Paul quotes verse 4 twice, arguing that those who preach the gospel should be supported by those they serve (1 Corinthians 9:9-10; 1 Timothy 5:18). He reads the ox law as expressing a principle of fairness that reaches beyond animals. Paul also records that he received forty lashes less one from Jewish authorities five times (2 Corinthians 11:24), a practice that kept safely under the limit of verse 3. The Sadducees questioned Jesus using the brother-in-law law, and he answered that in the resurrection people will not marry (Matthew 22:23-33). The levirate stories of Tamar and Ruth matter for the story of Jesus: both women appear in Matthew's genealogy (Matthew 1:3-5), and in each case a woman's courage kept the line of Judah alive when the men of the family failed. The link is historical and thematic rather than predictive.

hard.q: Why does the law command cutting off a woman's hand in verses 11-12, and why must Amalek's memory be blotted out?
hard.a:
Verses 11-12 contain the only mutilation penalty in Israel's law apart from the general talion formula, and it is jarring. Interpreters note that the offense threatened a man's ability to have children, which in Israel meant the survival of his name, the theme of the preceding law. Some Jewish interpreters in the rabbinic period read the penalty as a monetary fine for shame rather than a literal amputation, reasoning from the talion's treatment as compensation. Others take it literally as a deliberately severe deterrent. The text's harshness should be admitted, not explained away.

The command to blot out Amalek is also difficult. The text frames it as judgment on a people who attacked the weak without fear of God, and the Old Testament records Amalek as a repeated aggressor. Readers who find the conquest texts troubling will find this one troubling too, and the responses discussed under chapter 20 apply here as well. Jewish tradition has often read the command to remember Amalek as a charge to resist cruelty toward the defenseless in every generation, while Christians have generally read it as a command fulfilled in Israel's history and not a pattern for today.

questions: The law limited punishment so that a guilty man would not be degraded in your sight. How do you treat people who have clearly done wrong?
Paul applied the ox law to paying those who teach the gospel. How do you think about supporting people who serve you spiritually?
Amalek attacked the tired stragglers at the back. Who are the weary and struggling in your community, and who protects them?
